questions.q: In a perfectly competitive labour market, the wage is set by:
options: Demand for and supply of labour
questions.why: Each firm is a wage taker.

questions.q: A firm in a perfectly competitive labour market hires workers until:
questions.why: Beyond this, the next worker costs more than they add.

questions.q: All real-world labour markets are imperfectly competitive to some extent.
questions.why: The model is a yardstick, not a description.

questions.q: Fewer people train as plumbers, and demand is unchanged. What is the likely effect?
questions.why: Supply shifts left, which raises the wage and lowers employment.

questions.q: Match each fact to how it affects pay in the job.
pairs: Workers bring in a lot of revenue
Many people could do the job

questions.q: Explain why a top lawyer may earn more than a shop assistant in a competitive labour market.

ideas.label: The lawyer brings in more revenue, so demand or MRP is higher
Few people have the skills, so supply is low, while many can do shop work

questions.model: A top lawyer brings in a lot of revenue, so their MRP is high. Few people have the skills, so supply is low, whereas many people can work in a shop.
questions.why: High MRP plus scarce supply gives high pay.

tests.answer: A lawyer has a high MRP, and supply is low as few people have the skills.
A lawyer has a high MRP.
